13909-the-indiscretion-of-the-duchess-be:
Anthony Hope, author of The Prisoner of Zenda, wrote The Indiscretion of the Duchess in 1894. Two ladies, a nobleman, and a necklace drive the comedy of manners. Chapters promise a multitude of good reasons, a supper-table, and the unexpected that always happened. The duchess defines her position, retreats strategically, and faces an unparalleled insult.

A narrator, Gustave, and the duchess trade wit and schemes. An empty box, a timely truce, and a clever scheme turn the plot. Hope keeps the tone light, with romance under the farce. The novel shows his gift for Ruritanian-style intrigue in a modern setting. Fans of Hope will enjoy its pace and talk.
16007-the-dead-boxer-the-works-of-willia:
William Carleton's tale introduces a feared stranger known only as the Dead Boxer, a Black pugilist who drifts into Irish towns posting his challenge by night. No one ever sees how the notices appear, and local talk credits an evil spirit with the work. By local custom, a visiting boxer may claim fifty guineas if no townsman takes up his challenge within a set time.

The Dead Boxer always names the same ground for a fight: the town churchyard, beside a new grave dug at his own expense. Superstition, pride, and fear gather around him before a blow is struck. Carleton's story mixes folk belief with a sporting contest, giving readers a strange, eerie piece of old Irish storytelling.
16010-the-tithe-proctor-the-works-of-wil:
An Irish novel by William Carleton, The Tithe-Proctor, in his collected works. Carleton's preface rests the tale on a startling and extraordinary narrative, a document at once authentic and powerful. A gentleman of modest character, distinguished in a difficult branch of native literature, wrote the source. Carleton trusts readers will admit little more need be said.

The tithe-proctor, collector of the hated church tax, stands at the centre of Irish anger. His rounds through farms and cabins stir threats, plots, and violence. Carleton writes with fire for the peasantry and scorn for the system. The novel stands as a fierce Irish protest: a tax, a collector, and a people pushed to the edge.
16379-children-s-classics-in-dramatic-fo:
Augusta Stevenson turns Aesop's fables and folk tales into short plays for children in this 1908 book. The Clever Kid, The Wolf and the Horse, The Wise Crow, The Wolf and the Lamb, and The Blind Men and the Elephant lead the set. Lazy Kate, The Vain Jackdaw, and The Wish-Bird add German folk sources.

Each piece is short, with simple parts for school or home performance. Stevenson, a former Indianapolis teacher, keeps the morals clear and the humor gentle. The book suits teachers who want young actors to learn classic tales by playing them, not merely reading them.
19469-poems-teachers-ask-for-book-two:
Readers of a teachers' magazine chose the poems in this second volume, gathering more than two hundred pieces they had asked to see in print. The roll runs from Poe's Annabel Lee and Kipling's Ballad of East and West to schoolroom favorites on seasons, battles, and home life.

The set was made for classroom use: short, clear, and easy to recite, with an index of titles for quick finding. As a whole it shows what teachers of the time wanted children to carry in memory, from high verse to plain moral lyrics.
23138-diary-in-america-series-two:
Procrastination opens Diary in America, series two. Knowing a sight can be seen any time, the diarist reflects, people delay until they never see it at all. He recalls a lifelong Londoner who meant every year, for decades, to visit the Tower at last.

Frederick Marryat's second series continues his American tour, prisons, schools, and frontier settlements among its stops. The Tower joke does quiet work, a traveler's confession that familiarity blinds natives and visitors alike. Marryat writes as a naval officer abroad, direct about what he admires and what he finds absurd. Paired with the first series, the diary gives a full, opinionated portrait of Jacksonian America from a British deck, so to speak, still rolling under his sentences.
26364-reincarnation-and-the-law-of-karma:
William Walker Atkinson's Reincarnation and the Law of Karma, issued by the Yogi Publication Society in Chicago in 1908, studies rebirth and spiritual cause and effect as an old-new doctrine. Early chapters trace the belief through early races, Egyptians, Chaldeans, and Druids, then Romans and Greeks, with Pythagoras, Orpheus, and Plato in view.

Later parts cover Jews, Essenes, and early Christians, with Kabbalah teachings, and Hindus, called the mother of reincarnation. A modern West chapter treats the Theosophical Society, Madame Blavatsky, and Yogi philosophy. Theosophy, Atkinson reports, lists seven soul principles, from body and vitality to astral body, animal soul, human soul, spiritual soul, and spirit. The book states its doctrine as a system to weigh, not as proved fact.
2679-poems-by-emily-dickinson-series-two:
Emily Dickinson's poems, second series, gather the short, startling lyrics that she mostly kept private in life. Dickinson wrote in Amherst, in brief lines broken by dashes, about death, nature, faith, and the inner weather of a mind.

This series adds to the first a fresh set of her compressed masterpieces, where a slant of light or a fly's buzz can carry eternity. The poems demand slow reading, and they repay it with sudden clarity. The book belongs on any shelf of American poetry, as one of its founding voices.
27463-the-wonders-of-the-jungle-book-two:
Prince Sarath Ghosh wrote this children's reader as book two of The Wonders of the Jungle, in Heath's Supplementary Readers from D. C. Heath in 1918. Ghosh addresses children directly, promising many more wonders as he promised in book one, and urging them to think while they read.

Book one had promised more about elephants and the laws of their herd, and book two keeps that promise. It then turns to animals not described before: the tiger, the lion, the leopard, and the wolf. Ghosh shows how clever these animals are, and how some have affections just as people do. Young readers learn natural history by asking why animals act as they do.
30038-a-line-o-verse-or-two:
Bert Leston Taylor published A Line-o'-Verse or Two in Chicago in 1911, with the Reilly and Britton Company. Most of the rimes first ran in the Chicago Tribune and Puck, whose courtesy Taylor thanks for reprinting rights. The Lay of St. Ambrose is new. Taylor gives two reasons for gathering fugitive verse between covers. Naming a publisher beats searching dusty files when readers often ask for a copy of one jingle or another.

He dedicates the handful of rime joyously to his readers, a larger company with whom, through the Tribune, he has been on pleasant terms for years. The Lay of St. Ambrose opens the fun: Ambrose the anchorite, old and grey, larrups himself in his lonely cell, while lay-brothers wag their heads and say Ambrose has been at the bottle again. Taylor's verse is light, musical, and wry throughout.
30599-collected-poems-volume-two:
Alfred Noyes gathers his verse in Collected Poems, volume two, published in New York in October 1913 by Frederick A. Stokes, with copyrights from 1906 to 1913. Dramatic and acting rights are reserved, as in volume one, and applications for performance go to the publishers.

Contents open with Mist in the Valley, A Song of the Plough, The Banner, Rank and File, and The Sky-Lark Caged. Later poems add The Lovers' Flight, The Rock Pool, The Island Hawk, The Admiral's Ghost, Edinburgh, and a railway carriage scene. An East End coffee stall, Red of the Dawn, and further pieces follow. Noyes blends lyric, legend, and London life.
37063-george-morland-sixteen-examples-in:
Black of London issued this small book on George Morland in its British Artists line. Sixteen plates in colour show the painter's work, and Cuming wrote the opening essay. The Dipping-Well forms the cover plate, in Morland's country manner.

Confidences, owned by Mrs Carl Meyer, heads the list of plates. Idleness and Diligence, a matched pair, come next from Sir Edward Tennant's walls. Belinda, Billet-Doux follows, from Barratt's set. Morland painted inn yards, pigs, gypsies, and smugglers with a free, warm hand. His short, wild life ended in debt, yet his scenes of old rural England live in books like this, in true colour.
38558-the-white-crystals-being-an-accoun:
The White Crystals tells the adventures of two boys, by Howard Garis. Little, Brown of Boston brought the book out in October 1904. Bertha Corson Day drew the pictures that stand through the tale. Garis gives the book with love to his son Roger at the front. Twenty-five chapters run from the doctor's advice to a last wrestling match.

The salt city, a test of strength, and deep water fill the start. Gathering honey, a load of grapes, and lost on the mountain follow. Fighting a wild-cat and bad news raise the stakes in the middle. Copper and old bones, Jack Frost, and Lafayette Hill come next. A big black bear and queer operations crowd the later chapters. Roger suspects, plans, and journeys underneath the ground in that part. Digging for salt and plotters foiled close the boys' adventure out.
41383-punch-and-judy-with-instructions-h:
Thos A M Ward, an attorney at law, wrote Punch and Judy, with instructions how to manage the little wooden actors. It was printed at Janesville, Wisconsin, by Veeder and Leonard in eighteen seventy four. New and easy dialogues are arranged for beginners desirous to learn the puppets, the title page says. The shows are meant for Sunday schools, private parties, and parlor entertainments.

A preface reaches back to Egypt for the art. The invention of puppet shows carries us back long before the birth of Moses, Ward writes. Games enjoyed by the early people of Egypt were in their zenith in the reign of the Rameses, he says. Rameses the Second was a magnificent patron of letters as well as art, he notes. The Sacred Library Diodorus mentions has been discovered in his palace, he adds. Puppet players get a working Victorian handbook, with dialogues ready to perform.
43530-wood-carvings-in-english-churches-:
Francis Bond wrote this study of wood carvings in English churches. Oxford University Press issued it in 1910 with 124 photos and drawings. Part one treats stalls and tabernacle work in church wood. Part two treats bishops thrones and chancel chairs in turn.

Beverley Minster fronts the volume as its opening photo plate. Bond also wrote on fonts, misericords, and Westminster Abbey before. A church chest volume by Johnston stands in preparation in the set. Prices in shillings mark the companion volumes in the front list. The photos and drawings number one hundred twenty four in the volume as printed.
46503-gold-seeking-on-the-dalton-trail-b:
Arthur R Thompson wrote Gold-Seeking on the Dalton Trail, a boys’ tale of Alaska. Little, Brown, and Company issued the book in Boston in nineteen hundred. Two New England boys, the Bradfords, chase gold in the far north. Thompson gives the book to Dexter Wadleigh Lewis, his camp fire mate.

A letter from Alaska sets the lads to buy their full outfit at home. Seattle, Pyramid Harbor, and the first camp mark the road north. Sledding up the Chilkat vale and the pass summit tax their strength. A great nugget, heard of from Uncle Will, draws them ever on. Claims are staked at Dalton’s Post and a snug cabin built for frost. Roly is hurt, a fire strikes camp, and ice traps their path. Duck hunts, a bear skin, and a wolf raid fill the wild months. Robbers at last, then Skagway and Dyea close the long trek.
46800-the-legendary-history-of-the-cross:
Legendary History of the Cross is a picture book of sixty four woodcuts with text by John Ashton. The cuts come from a Dutch book issued by Veldener in the year 1483. Baring Gould wrote a preface for the London edition of 1887 in old style print. Its preface warns that the origin of the medieval romance of the cross is hard to find.

That romance told how the wood of the cross grew from Eden through sacred history. Kings, queens, and wonders crowd the tale the Dutch cuts show scene by scene. Ashton introduction and notes guide readers through each archaic image in the series. Lovers of folklore and old print gain a famed legend in its picture form.
56197-cupid-s-fair-weather-booke-includi:
John Cecil Clay and Oliver Herford made Cupid’s Fair-Weather Booke for lovers. Charles Scribner’s Sons issued the gay book in New York in nineteen hundred eleven. Daniel Cupid lends his name as guide of the whole work. An almanack for any two years stands in its long title.

True love ought to last that long, the title page jokes in print. The craft it teaches bears the coined name of hearticulture here. Hope vines die of late frosts if set out too soon, it warns. Young plants need warmth and care, and chill kills them fast. January’s forecast tells of brain storms and cold good resolves. Ice water pours, then brighter days lift the glass once more. Saint Valentine goes fishing in the February sign of the Fishes. Each month pairs its star sign with a lover’s weather chart.
58887-aviation-in-canada-1917-1918-being:
Aviation in Canada, 1917-1918, records the work of the Royal Air Force in Canada. Alan Sullivan, a lieutenant in that force, compiled the account. Rous and Mann printed it at Toronto in 1919. A note warns that the Air Ministry is not responsible for its statements. The Imperial Munitions Board and Canadian Aeroplanes share the story.

The contents map a training empire. Chapters treat headquarters, camps, and schools in turn. Beamsville and Camp Borden earn their own accounts. The instructor and the medical service receive chapters. Winter flying and flying accidents follow. Gunnery, wireless, and photography each get a section. The opening chapter sets the scene at the Western Front in 1916. The Somme fighting led to the corps' formation in Canada.
59947-hubbell-trading-post-national-hist:
The Hubbell Trading Post Junior Ranger Workbook is an activity book of the National Park Service. It serves the historic site at Ganado, Arizona. Children complete it at the visitor centre. Answers can be found in the exhibits, it says. A ranger checks the finished book at the desk. The first tasks ask what a Navajo trader brought long ago. Wool, rugs, and food goods were the classic trade items.

Matching tasks test names and dates of the site. What the Navajo call themselves is one item. The family burial ground is another. The hogan, the six or ten-sided home, is asked after. Navajo code talkers of the war appear as well. The year John Lorenzo Hubbell came to Ganado is a key date. Workbooks of this kind turn a visit into a lesson. The trading post still stands as a working store.
65120-harper-s-household-handbook-a-guid:
Harper's Household Handbook, a guide to easy ways of doing woman's work, was published by Harper and Brothers in New York in 1913. The title page promises method rather than drudgery. Its first chapter joins wash-day wisdom to nursing and the sickroom. That pairing shows the book's range: the whole management of a house, from laundry tub to invalid's bedside, between two covers.

Handbooks of this kind sold alongside Harper's cookery and baby books, advertised in the front pages here. The age was professionalising housework. Domestic science promised that system could lighten labour, and publishers built whole shelves of such counsel for women who ran houses without the servants their mothers had. The handbook survives as a record of what a well-run American home was supposed to require in 1913.
67969-phallic-worship-a-description-of-t:
Phallic Worship, a description of the mysteries of the sex worship of the ancients, was privately printed in London in 1880. The book adds a history of the masculine cross. It treats early symbolism, Hebrew rites, Bacchic feasts, and the mysteries of the ancient faiths, at form level.

The opening chapter holds that sex worship ruled among all peoples of ancient times. It was often mixed with star, serpent, and tree worship. The powers of nature were given human feelings, passions, and acts. Whether the sun, the serpent, or the emblem was praised, the thought was one, praise of the making power of life. The writer traces the creeds of old nations to one source, the worship of nature forces, with sun worship at the root. Students of old faiths get a Victorian study, frankly printed for private readers.
68623-educated-working-women-essays-on-t:
Clara E Collet wrote Educated Working Women, essays on the work place of women workers in the middle classes, issued at London in 1902. Collet was a Fellow of University College London. The book is given to the memory of Frances Mary Buss. Six essays fill the volume, each first read or printed in a journal.

The lead essay was read to the South Place Ethical Society in 1890. One essay weighs the prospects of marriage for women. One tracks how middle class working women spend their pay. Age limits for women and Mrs Stetson's ideal get essays too. A last essay traces fifty years of growth for women in work. A verse from Browning heads the praise of deed over speech.
69485-letters-on-the-equality-of-the-sex:
Letters on the Equality of the Sexes and the Condition of Woman is a landmark tract written as letters to a friend. Isaac Knapp published the book at Boston in 1838. The letters are addressed to Mary Parker, president of the Boston Female Anti-Slavery Society. The first letter is dated from Amesbury in July 1837.

The writer owns that the ground is nearly untrodden. The case rests on the Bible alone, read in its original tongues. The English version is denied as inspired, and the writer claims the right to judge its meaning at first hand. The first letter treats the original equality of woman at creation. God made man in his image and gave dominion to them alike, the argument runs. The letters grew from the antislavery fight into a founding text of the women's rights cause.
70944-knock-three-one-two:
Knock Three-One-Two is a crime tale by Fredric Brown, out in nineteen fifty-nine. A short form ran that year in a tale sheet past the name Night of the Psycho. Brown was known for a shelf of crime tales with coined names. The tale opens at five of the clock on a man the press calls the psycho, past his next slay but two months.

He stands in the hall of a flat block past a door, his hands in a flex and rest past his strained nerves. Those hands are vast strong hands of a choke man that have slain past twice. The need to harm and slay a wife is on him once more that night. The law men call him by that same short name while they strain to learn his true one in time.
74345-the-aldine-speller-part-two:
Bryce and Sherman made this Aldine Speller, part two, for schools. Newson printed it in New York in 1916 for grades three, four. Bryce served Minneapolis schools, Sherman had led Monson, Massachusetts schools. Directions to teachers open the book on oral spelling first.

Oral spelling should precede written work in primary grades, they write. Clear pronunciation must come before a child spells a word aloud. Mere hearing of lessons is a thing of the past, they say. Interest is nine tenths of education in spelling, they contend. Review lessons serve as the true tests in their plan of spelling teaching.
75507-pistols-for-two:
Pistols for Two is a book of short prose by Owen Hatteras, put out at New York in the late nineteen teens. Its parts are two long portraits, each named for a man of letters of the day. The first takes up a famed critic and stage hand of New York.

The prose that starts the first sketch sets its sharp key at once. Life tales fail, it says, as mind science fails, since both oft take a maze for a light. The aim of a life tale is to show a whole man. Its fruit is oft to make him a sealed maze, a wax doll smooth as glass and as dead as a pickled gherkin. True sense of a man comes by no such drain of facts, the piece holds.
78631-tippecanoe-and-cougars-two:
Tippecanoe and Cougars Two is a humorous western tale by Tuttle. Tuttle also wrote Sparing the Family Tree and Figures of Speech. The narrator opens in this vale of tears with a wide complaint. He has met a lot of fools come from the ends of earth. They did injury to his nervous system, he says, yet he survived.

His carcass stays out of the loco lodge in spite of their doings. Some fools are of the common or hillside variety, he allows there. Others are of educated stock, peculiar to look upon and to hear. To all ye fools he offers a place at his table freely. But the absent minded must vamoose, for their days are few.
78749-coffin-for-two:
Winston K Marks brings a Venus prospector home to a changed Earth in a short tale. The narrator has spent three years alone in Callispo Valley. Two tons of uranium concentrate paid for the trip.

Albany Field's lights make him nearly weep. He checks his cargo by short-wave and hands over the forty-ton crate. Fourteen inches of beard shake out as he climbs down. A blond surface jockey greets him, not a robot. The man wears a red star on his forehead. The headnote gives the twist plainly. Gwen waited in his heart, but Gwen had no heart, and a star on her brow. Marks wrote many such twist tales for the science fiction magazines of the day.
9465-songs-of-two:
Arthur Sherburne Hardy put out Songs of Two in 1900, a slim book of short love poems. The poems come in numbered parts, each one brief and plain in form. Most speak straight to a loved one, called Dear, in a warm and close voice. Love, parting, trust, and hope run through the whole set.

One poem dreams of death and wakes to a loved voice. Others weigh what it means to give and to wait, or to walk apart for a time. A flower in the woods, a spring, and a dawn sky stand for feelings that plain words fail to hold. A reader gets a quiet, tender look at love as a day to day bond, not a grand show.
britannica-1911-kuro-siwo: The Kuro Siwo, or Kuro Shio, a name meaning "blue salt," is a stream current in the Pacific Ocean. Its warm water and blue colour set it apart. It flows north-eastwards along the east coast of Japan, with a strip of cold water between it and the shore. The current holds together as a stream until about 40 degrees north, between 150 and 160 degrees east. There it melts into the easterly drift of the North Pacific. The Kuro Siwo is the Pacific match of the Gulf Stream in the Atlantic.
children-s-classics-in-dramatic-form-boo:
Book Two of Augusta Stevenson's dramatic reader appeared in 1908, again built for schoolchildren to perform. Short plays carry time and place headings and simple sets. Most are marked as suggested by a source tale, rather than adapted word for word. Aesop dominates the early pages, as he did in the first book.

Wolves meet a kid, a horse, and a lamb in the opening plays. A crow drops pebbles into a pitcher. The shepherd-boy calls wolf once too often. German folk tales add Lazy Kate, two millers, and a proud ring-finger. The blind men and the elephant come from a folk story. Pocahontas saving Jamestown, Pocahontas and Captain Smith, and King Alfred burning the cakes close the book in history and legend.
doe-osti-3001974-remote-autonomous-vehic:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory staff Doug Mann, Aaron O'Toole, Tyler Waddle, and Andrew Duncan present RAVEN in a November 2025 report. RAVEN, the Remote Autonomous Vehicle Extended Network, is a software platform for flying drones beyond the operator's line of sight. Such flights need special waivers and strong safety checks under Federal Aviation Administration rules. Weak long-range radio links are the main technical hurdle.

RAVEN replaces ORNL's 2019 MAVNet system, which offered backup links over local networks, cell service, and satellite but grew hard to maintain. The new platform adds room to grow, live alerts, and feeds of detection and airspace data. It also lays groundwork for counter-drone work. Future plans add standard interfaces so language models can query the data sources.
doe-osti-3012343-vrn3p-variational-recur:
Day ahead net load under heavy solar penetration is forecast with a variational recurrent neural network in PNNL-38890, the VRN3P final report. Soumya Kundu led a Pacific Northwest National Laboratory team with Lawrence Livermore and Portland General Electric partners. The project period ran from February 2021 to September 2023.

Validation ran in GridLAB-D on anonymised real solar, net load, and end use data at 20 to 50 percent annual solar energy. Objectives covered capturing uncertainty, deployability, and interpretability of the deep model. The GRAF-Plan tool then estimated how better forecasts cut balancing reserve procurement. Sensitivity analysis includes second order terms that standard treatments drop.
doe-osti-3017992-hydrogen-infrastructure:
Justin Bracci, Logan Martens, Son Tran, and ten National Laboratory of the Rockies colleagues wrote this February 2026 report, NLR/TP-5700-91612, on hydrogen infrastructure analysis frameworks for aviation. Airports are a plausible early hydrogen market, but they concentrate the hard problems: making, moving, storing, and dispensing a very light, very cold fuel inside a safety-critical facility.

The report assembles the analysis frameworks an airport planner needs, from demand and supply modeling to safety layout. One detailed thread covers storage setbacks. The text walks through the national fire code, NFPA 2, and its minimum setback distances for bulk liquid hydrogen storage. Every airport is urged to layer its own safety judgment on top of those minimums. Figures chart the distances involved. For airport authorities and fuel providers sketching hydrogen service, this is the reference that turns enthusiasm into checklists.
doe-osti-3023050-reopt-federal-user-supp:
Slides from the second REopt federal user support session, held September 10, 2025. They were presented by Valerie Michel of FEMP with Kathleen Krah, Bill Becker, and Dan Olis of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory. REopt is an energy planning tool that helps sites weigh renewable energy, storage, and heating options. The session aimed to build user skill and gather feedback on future support.

The agenda pairs a capability overview and live demo with training on evaluating heat pumps inside the REopt web tool. Screens show how air-source and ground-source heat pumps are selected for space heating and hot water. A federal success story covers a ground-source heat pump project at the Denver Federal Center, and discussion and questions close the session.
doe-osti-3452165-cast-technical-bulletin:
Oak Ridge technical bulletin ORNL/SPR-2026/4615, number 013, tests a two-way satellite time transfer network across spread-out sites. Tyler McCormick, Amir Osman, and Chris Cooper wrote the bulletin. Satellite navigation timing can be jammed or spoofed, so a backup method matters.

Two-way satellite transfer can rival navigation system accuracy, the bulletin states. Analysts trimmed the data set to cut volume and clarify plots. They then removed the median time gap from each point. The final plots show total offset swing across the collection period. Timing labs gain proof that a non-GNSS path can hold precise time.
nasa-tm-19670030822-standard-payload-mod:
Preston T. Farish, of NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, wrote this planning memorandum on July 22, 1965. It presents a standard definition network for payload module work, covering project Phases A through D. A definition network maps the tasks and decisions that turn an idea into approved hardware.

Farish offers the information as a guideline for managers. Its aim is the soundest practical management baseline for planning, approval, and execution of future programs. The standard payload module is the example throughout. The abstract promises the network and concept proposal, with early definition material, as the core of the document.
podcast-joerogan-9-z0kglwpwo:
Gerontologist Aubrey de Grey joins Joe Rogan for episode 1432 of the Joe Rogan Experience. De Grey is a top voice for the claim that aging is a disease that can be cured. His work aims to fix the harm that builds in cells with age.

De Grey lays out the seven kinds of cell harm he says drive old age and death. He argues each can be fixed with care that is near at hand. Rogan asks when a normal man might see such care. Listeners get the boldest case in the youth field. The library keeps the episode as a record of his stated work.
podcast-tuckercarlson-YGRMp-GkIwo:
Strategist Steve Bannon talks with Tucker Carlson after a court orders him to prison. Bannon had refused a subpoena from the January 6 panel. He presents the sentence as political punishment.

He stays defiant in tone from the first minute. The title calls his reply the subject, and nothing else crowds it. Bannon vows that prison will not silence his movement work. Carlson treats him as a prisoner of conscience. The episode preserves a key ally's last public stand before serving time, aimed at loyal fans. His base hears a call to keep fighting.
poems-by-emily-dickinson-series-two:
Emily Dickinson's second series of Poems followed the success of the first posthumous volume, bringing more of her manuscripts into print. Dickinson had spent her life in Amherst, Massachusetts, writing lyrics of extraordinary compression and keeping them in hand-sewn packets at home. The first series proved that readers existed for this strange, private work; a second helping followed at once.

Like its predecessor, the volume draws on the store of poems she left behind, treating the same great subjects. Death and immortality, the natural world watched from a garden, love, pain, and the life of the mind. Her habits are all here, the dashes, the capital letters mid-line, the hymns that swerve into doubt. Together the early series built the reading public that made Dickinson a central American poet.
poems-teachers-ask-for-book-two:
Teachers chose the contents of this anthology themselves. Poems Teachers Ask For, Book Two, gathers more than two hundred poems that readers of the magazine Normal Instructor-Primary Plans had requested for its page of poems readers asked for. The result is a working schoolroom library: the pieces American teachers actually reached for when they needed a poem for a holiday. A memorial, a recitation, or a rainy Friday afternoon.

The index reads like a roll of the era's school canon: Poe's Annabel Lee, Kipling's Ballad of East and West. Tennyson's Break, Break, Break, Whittier's Barbara Frietchie in the companion tradition, and patriotic set pieces for flag days. Sentimental, moral, and seasonal poems fill the rest, each with a classroom use. Books like this one, chosen from below by working teachers, show what poetry meant in ordinary American schools before the anthology trade professionalized the canon.
songs-of-two:
Arthur Sherburne Hardy dates Songs of Two to 1900, and the poems speak in a lover's voice of parting and faith. The first poem dreams that the singer is dead and hears a footstep on the sod above. The Dear one touches his breast and asks what she shall write against his name for men to see. Quick comes the answer: I was beloved of thee.

The second poem looks down a path that splits, where the two must walk alone a little space. The singer vows to wait strong with memory alone till he sees her face. Yet he turns, in sore need, to beg her giving grace once more. At the last parting, when night hides her smile, his hand shall seek her own and hold it fast.
the-dead-boxer-the-works-of-william-carl:
William Carleton's The Dead Boxer opens one evening near the end of April in the beginning of the eighteenth century, about the year 1720 by the narrator's guess. A young man named Lamh Laudher O'Rorke, or Strong-handed O'Rorke, walks with a stout oaken cudgel. He heads toward an orchard at the skirt of a country town in a part of Ireland left nameless.

His Christian name is John, Carleton explains. Irish families of one name were told apart by nicknames drawn from build, speed, or look: swift Paddy, yellow Jack, big Michael, red James. John and his forefathers earned theirs through great bodily strength and courage. The pale sun hangs over western hills as he saunters, slow with quiet delight in the opening summer. He meets a stout, muscular older woman in a red woollen petticoat and blue hose, carrying a short oaken staff.
the-indiscretion-of-the-duchess-being-a-: Anthony Hope wrote this tale, published in New York in 1894. He was the author of The Prisoner of Zenda. The subtitle promises two ladies, a nobleman, and a necklace. A frontispiece caption shows a fight on the sands. The narrator flings a man off the duke there. Only the title page and contents are present here. The narrative itself does not appear. The headings promise a supper-table's meaning. The duchess defines her position. Something is heard through a door. An insult, a clever scheme, and an empty box follow.
the-tithe-proctor-the-works-of-william-c:
William Carleton's Tithe-Proctor, in volume two of his works, is founded on a startling narrative document that Carleton says leaves him little to add. His preface promises a fair and impartial hand in depicting the Tithe Rebellion's tumults and massacres. He begs any party feeling hurt to blame the claims of truth and justice, not a wish to offend. Ireland's tithe contentions, he admits, have bitterly distracted the unhappy country.

Carleton confesses one liberty: the murder of the Bolands happened in 1808 and the Carrickshock massacre in 1832, so he moved dates to join them in one story. That candour typifies his approach, documentary evidence inside fiction. Readers of Irish history get a novelist close to the peasants he portrays, explaining his evidence before the tale of a tithe collector begins.
